blocks.p: The angel Michael continues from the Flood to tell what will follow; then, in speaking of Abraham, he comes by degrees to explain who that seed of the woman will be, which was promised to Adam and Eve at the Fall: his incarnation, death, resurrection, and ascension, and the state of the Church until his second coming. Adam, greatly satisfied and comforted by these accounts and promises, goes down the hill with Michael. He wakes Eve, who all this while had slept, but with gentle dreams that had calmed her to quietness of mind and submission. Michael takes them one in each hand and leads them out of Paradise, the fiery sword waving behind them, and the cherubim taking their stations to guard the place.

v: As one who on a journey stops at noon,
Though bent on speed, so here the archangel paused
Between the world destroyed and world restored,
Should Adam wish perhaps to interpose;
Then, with transition sweet, resumes his speech:
“So you have seen one world begin and end,
And man, as from a second stock, proceed.
Much you have yet to see, but I perceive
Your mortal sight is failing; things divine
Must surely dim and weary human sense.
Henceforth what is to come I will relate;
You therefore give due hearing, and attend.
“This second source of men, while yet but few,
And while the dread of judgment past remains
Fresh in their minds, fearing the Deity,
With some regard to what is just and right
Shall lead their lives, and multiply apace,
Laboring the soil, and reaping plenteous crops,
Grain, wine, and oil; and from the herd or flock,
And sacrificing bullock, lamb, or kid,
With large wine offerings poured, and sacred feasts,
Shall spend their days in blameless joy, and dwell
Long time in peace by families and tribes
Under paternal rule; till one shall rise
Of proud, ambitious heart, who, not content
With fair equality, fraternal state,
Will arrogate dominion undeserved
Over his brothers, and quite dispossess
Concord and law of nature from the earth;
Hunting (and men, not beasts, shall be his game)
With war and hostile snare all who refuse
Subjection to his tyrannous domain.
A mighty hunter so he shall be called
Before the Lord, as if in spite of Heaven,
Or claiming from Heaven a second sovereignty;
And from rebellion he shall take his name,
Though he accuses others of rebellion.
He, with a crew whom like ambition joins
With him or under him to tyrannize,
Marching from Eden toward the west, shall find
The plain where, black and bubbling, liquid pitch
Boils out from underground, the mouth of Hell.
Of brick, and of that stuff, they plan to build
A city and tower whose top may reach to Heaven,
And get themselves a name, lest, far dispersed
In foreign lands, their memory be lost,
Regardless whether good or evil fame.
But God, who often stoops to visit men
Unseen, and through their habitations walks
To mark their doings, soon beholding them,
Comes down to see their city, before the tower
Obstructs Heaven’s towers, and in derision sets
Upon their tongues a diverse spirit, to raze
Quite out their native language, and instead
To sow a jangling noise of words unknown.
At once a hideous gabble rises loud
Among the builders; each to the other calls,
Not understood, till, hoarse and all in rage,
As mocked, they storm. Great laughter was in Heaven,
As they looked down to see the hubbub strange
And hear the din: thus was the building left
Ridiculous, and the work Confusion named.”
To which thus Adam, fatherly displeased:
“O execrable son, so to aspire
Above his brothers, claiming for himself
Authority usurped, from God not given!
He gave us only over beast, fish, fowl
Dominion absolute; that right we hold
By his donation; but man over men
He made no lord; such title for himself
Reserving, human left from human free.
But this usurper’s proud encroachment stops
Not at mankind; his tower intends toward God
Siege and defiance. Wretched man! What food
Will he bring up so high to keep alive
Himself and his rash army, where thin air
Above the clouds will starve his entrails gross,
And famish him of breath, if not of bread?”
To whom thus Michael: “Justly you abhor
That son, who on the quiet state of men
Such trouble brought, attempting to subdue
Rational liberty; yet know as well,
Since your original lapse, true liberty
Is lost, which with right reason always dwells
Twinned, and from her has no separate being:
Reason in man obscured, or not obeyed,
Immediately inordinate desires
And upstart passions seize the government
From reason, and reduce to servitude
Man, free till then. Therefore, since he permits
Within himself unworthy powers to reign
Over free reason, God, in judgment just,
Subjects him from without to violent lords,
Who often, as unjustly, will enthrall
His outward freedom. Tyranny must be,
Though for the tyrant that is no excuse.
Yet sometimes nations will decline so low
From virtue, which is reason, that no wrong,
But justice, and some fatal curse attached,
Deprives them of their outward liberty,
Their inward lost: witness the irreverent son
Of him who built the ark, who, for the shame
Done to his father, heard this heavy curse,
‘Servant of servants,’ on his vicious race.
“Thus will this latter, like the former world,
Still tend from bad to worse, till God at last,
Wearied with their iniquities, withdraws
His presence from among them, and averts
His holy eyes, resolving from then on
To leave them to their own polluted ways,
And one peculiar nation to select
From all the rest, by whom he’ll be invoked,
A nation from one faithful man to spring:
Him, on this side Euphrates still residing,
Bred up in idol worship. Oh, that men
(Can you believe it?) should have grown so dull,
While yet the patriarch lived, saved from the Flood,
As to forsake the living God, and fall
To worship their own work in wood and stone
For gods! Yet him the Most High God will deign
To call by vision from his father’s house,
His kindred, and false gods, into a land
Which he will show him, and from him will raise
A mighty nation, and upon him shower
His benediction so, that in his seed
All nations shall be blessed; at once he obeys,
Not knowing to what land, yet firmly trusts.
I see him, but you cannot, with what faith
He leaves his gods, his friends, and native soil,
Ur of Chaldea, passing now the ford
To Haran, after him a cumbrous train
Of herds and flocks, and servants without number;
Not wandering poor, but trusting all his wealth
With God, who called him, in a land unknown.
“Canaan he now attains; I see his tents
Pitched around Sechem, and the neighboring plain
Of Moreb; there by promise he receives
Gift to his progeny of all that land,
From Hamath northward to the desert south
(Things by their names I call, though yet unnamed),
From Hermon east to the great western sea.
Mount Hermon, yonder sea, each place behold
In prospect, as I point them: on the shore,
Mount Carmel; here, the double-fountained stream,
Jordan, true limit eastward; but his sons
Shall dwell to Senir, that long ridge of hills.
Ponder this well: all nations of the earth
Shall in his seed be blessed; and by that seed
Is meant your great deliverer, who shall bruise
The Serpent’s head; of which, a little later,
More plainly you shall hear. This patriarch blessed,
Whom faithful Abraham the years will call,
A son, and of his son a grandchild, leaves,
Like him in faith, in wisdom, and renown;
The grandchild, with twelve sons increased, departs
From Canaan to a land hereafter called
Egypt, divided by the river Nile.
See where it flows, disgorging at seven mouths
Into the sea. To sojourn in that land
He comes, invited by a younger son
In time of dearth, a son whose worthy deeds
Raise him to be the second in that realm
Of Pharaoh. There he dies, and leaves his race
Growing into a nation, and, now grown,
Suspected by a later king, who seeks
To check their overgrowth, as guests within
Too numerous; so of guests he makes them slaves
Inhospitably, and kills their infant males,
Till by two brothers (those two brothers call
Moses and Aaron), sent from God to claim
His people from enslavement, they return
With glory and spoil back to their promised land.
“But first the lawless tyrant, who denies
To know their God, or give his message heed,
Must be compelled by signs and judgments dire:
To blood unshed the rivers must be turned;
Frogs, lice, and flies must all his palace fill
With loathed intrusion, and fill all the land;
His cattle must of rot and murrain die;
Boils and blisters must cover all his flesh,
And all his people’s; thunder mixed with hail,
Hail mixed with fire, must tear the Egyptian sky
And wheel on earth, devouring where it rolls;
What it devours not, herb, or fruit, or grain,
A darkening cloud of locusts swarming down
Must eat, and on the ground leave nothing green;
Darkness must overshadow all his bounds,
Palpable darkness, and blot out three days;
Last, with one midnight stroke, all the firstborn
Of Egypt must lie dead. Thus with ten wounds
This river-dragon, tamed at length, submits
To let his sojourners depart, and often
Humbles his stubborn heart, but still, like ice
More hardened after thaw; till, in his rage
Pursuing those he just dismissed, the sea
Swallows him with his host, but lets them pass
As on dry land between two crystal walls,
Awed by the rod of Moses so to stand
Divided, till the rescued gain their shore.
Such wondrous power God to his saint will lend,
Though present in his angel, who shall go
Before them in a cloud and pillar of fire,
By day a cloud, by night a pillar of fire,
To guide them on their journey, and remove
Behind them while the obdurate king pursues.
All night he will pursue, but his approach
Darkness defends between till morning watch;
Then through the fiery pillar and the cloud
God, looking forth, will trouble all his host
And break their chariot wheels; when, by command,
Moses once more extends his potent rod
Over the sea; the sea his rod obeys;
On their embattled ranks the waves return
And overwhelm their host. The chosen race
Safe toward Canaan from the shore advance
Through the wild desert, not the readiest way,
Lest, entering on the Canaanites, alarmed,
War frighten them, still inexpert, and fear
And send them back to Egypt, choosing rather
Inglorious life with servitude; for life
To noble and ignoble is more sweet
Untrained in arms, where rashness does not drive.
“This also they shall gain by their delay
In the wide wilderness: there they shall found
Their government, and their great senate choose
Through the twelve tribes, to rule by laws ordained.
God from the Mount of Sinai, whose gray top
Shall tremble at his coming, will himself
In thunder, lightning, and loud trumpets’ sound
Ordain them laws, part such as may pertain
To civil justice, part religious rites
Of sacrifice, informing them, by types
And shadows, of that destined seed to bruise
The Serpent, by what means he shall achieve
Mankind’s deliverance. But the voice of God
To mortal ear is dreadful; they beseech
That Moses might report to them his will,
And terror cease; he grants them their desire,
Instructed that to God is no access
Without a mediator, whose high office
Moses now bears in figure, to introduce
One greater, of whose day he shall foretell,
And all the prophets in their age the times
Of great Messiah shall sing. Thus, laws and rites
Established, such delight has God in men
Obedient to his will, that he will deign
Among them to set up his tabernacle,
The Holy One with mortal men to dwell.
By his command a sanctuary is framed
Of cedar, overlaid with gold; in it
An ark, and in the ark his testimony,
The records of his covenant; over these
A mercy seat of gold, between the wings
Of two bright cherubim; before him burn
Seven lamps, as in a zodiac representing
The heavenly fires; over the tent a cloud
Shall rest by day, a fiery gleam by night,
Except on journeys; and at length they come,
Conducted by his angel, to the land
Promised to Abraham and his seed. The rest
Were long to tell: how many battles fought,
How many kings destroyed, and kingdoms won,
Or how the sun shall in mid-heaven stand still
A day entire, and night’s due course adjourn,
Man’s voice commanding, ‘Sun, in Gibeon stand,
And you, Moon, in the vale of Aialon,’
Till Israel overcomes; so call the third
From Abraham, son of Isaac, and from him
His whole descent, who thus shall Canaan win.”
Here Adam interposed: “O sent from Heaven,
Enlightener of my darkness, gracious things
You have revealed, those chiefly which concern
Just Abraham and his seed. Now first I find
My eyes’ true opening, my heart much eased,
Lately perplexed with thoughts of what would come
To me and all mankind; but now I see
His day, in whom all nations shall be blessed,
Favor unmerited by me, who sought
Forbidden knowledge by forbidden means.
This yet I fail to grasp: why, then, to those
Among whom God will deign to dwell on earth
So many and such various laws are given;
So many laws imply so many sins
Among them: how can God with such reside?”
To whom thus Michael: “Do not doubt that sin
Will reign among them, as begotten of you;
And therefore law was given them to prove
Their natural depravity, by stirring up
Sin against law to fight, that when they see
Law can lay bare their sin, but not remove,
Save by those shadowy expiations weak,
The blood of bulls and goats, they may conclude
Some blood more precious must be paid for man,
Just for unjust, that in such righteousness,
To them by faith imputed, they may find
Justification toward God, and peace
Of conscience, which the law by ceremonies
Cannot appease, nor man the moral part
Perform, and not performing cannot live.
So law appears imperfect, and but given
With purpose to resign them, in full time,
Up to a better covenant, disciplined
From shadowy types to truth, from flesh to spirit,
From imposition of strict laws to free
Acceptance of large grace, from servile fear
To filial, works of law to works of faith.
And therefore shall not Moses, though by God
Highly beloved, being but the minister
Of law, his people into Canaan lead;
But Joshua, whom the Gentiles Jesus call,
His name and office bearing, who shall quell
The adversary Serpent, and bring back
Through the world’s wilderness long-wandering man
Safe to eternal Paradise of rest.
“Meanwhile they, in their earthly Canaan placed,
Long time shall dwell and prosper; but when sins
National interrupt their public peace,
Provoking God to raise them enemies,
From whom, as often, he saves them penitent,
By judges first, then under kings; of whom
The second, both for piety renowned
And mighty deeds, a promise shall receive
Irrevocable, that his royal throne
Forever shall endure; the like shall sing
All prophecy: that of the royal stock
Of David (so I name this king) shall rise
A son, the woman’s seed foretold to you,
Foretold to Abraham, in whom shall trust
All nations, and to kings foretold, of kings
The last, for of his reign shall be no end.
But first a long succession must ensue;
And his next son, for wealth and wisdom famed,
The clouded ark of God, till then in tents
Wandering, shall in a glorious temple enshrine.
Such follow him as shall be registered
Part good, part bad, of bad the longer scroll,
Whose foul idolatries and other faults,
Heaped on the people’s sins, will so incense
God as to leave them, and expose their land,
Their city, his temple, and his holy ark,
With all his sacred things, a scorn and prey
To that proud city whose high walls you saw
Left in confusion, and called Babylon.
There in captivity he lets them dwell
The space of seventy years, then brings them back,
Remembering mercy, and his covenant sworn
To David, established as the days of Heaven.
Returned from Babylon by leave of kings,
Their lords, whom God disposed, the house of God
They first rebuild, and for a little while
In humble state live modestly, till, grown
In wealth and multitude, factious they grow;
But first among the priests dissension springs,
Men who attend the altar, and should most
Endeavor peace: their strife pollution brings
Upon the temple itself; at last they seize
The scepter, and ignore the sons of David,
Then lose it to a stranger, that the true
Anointed King Messiah might be born
Barred of his right; yet at his birth a star,
Unseen before in heaven, proclaims him come,
And guides the Eastern sages, who inquire
His place, to offer incense, myrrh, and gold;
His place of birth a solemn angel tells
To simple shepherds, keeping watch by night;
They gladly hurry there, and by a choir
Of squadroned angels hear his carol sung.
A virgin is his mother, but his sire
The Power of the Most High; he shall ascend
The throne hereditary, and bound his reign
With earth’s wide bounds, his glory with the heavens.”
He ceased, discerning Adam with such joy
So overcharged, it would like grief have wept
Without the vent of words, which these he breathed:
“O prophet of glad tidings, finisher
Of utmost hope! Now clear I understand
What my best thoughts have often sought in vain:
Why our great expectation should be called
The seed of woman. Virgin mother, hail,
High in the love of Heaven! Yet from my loins
You shall proceed, and from your womb the Son
Of God Most High: so God with man unites.
Now must the Serpent his capital bruise
Expect with mortal pain. Say where and when
Their fight, what stroke shall bruise the victor’s heel.”
To whom thus Michael: “Do not dream their fight
Is like a duel, or the local wounds
Of head or heel: not for this joins the Son
Manhood to Godhead, with more strength to foil
Your enemy; nor thus is overcome
Satan, whose fall from Heaven, a deadlier bruise,
Did not prevent his dealing you death’s wound;
Which he who comes, your Savior, shall make whole,
Not by destroying Satan, but his works
In you and in your seed. Nor can this be,
Except by his fulfilling what you lacked,
Obedience to the law of God, imposed
On penalty of death, and suffering death,
The penalty to your transgression due,
And due to theirs which out of yours will grow:
So only can high justice rest repaid.
The law of God exact he shall fulfill
Both by obedience and by love, though love
Alone fulfills the law; your punishment
He shall endure by coming in the flesh
To a reproachful life and cursed death,
Proclaiming life to all who shall believe
In his redemption, and that his obedience,
Imputed, becomes theirs by faith, his merits
To save them, not their own, though works of law.
For this he shall live hated, be blasphemed,
Seized on by force, judged, and to death condemned,
A death of shame and curse, nailed to the cross
By his own nation, slain for bringing life;
But to the cross he nails your enemies,
The law that is against you, and the sins
Of all mankind, with him there crucified,
Never to hurt them more who rightly trust
In this his satisfaction. So he dies,
But soon revives; Death over him no power
Shall long usurp; before the third dawn’s light
Returns, the morning stars shall see him rise
Out of his grave, fresh as the dawning light,
Your ransom paid, which man from death redeems,
His death for man, as many as offered life
Do not neglect, and the benefit embrace
By faith not void of works. This godlike act
Annuls your doom, the death you should have died,
In sin forever lost from life; this act
Shall bruise the head of Satan, crush his strength,
Defeating Sin and Death, his two main arms,
And fix far deeper in his head their stings
Than temporal death shall bruise the victor’s heel,
Or theirs whom he redeems, a death like sleep,
A gentle wafting to immortal life.
“Nor after resurrection shall he stay
Longer on earth than certain times to appear
To his disciples, men who in his life
Still followed him; to them he leaves in charge
To teach all nations what of him they learned
And his salvation, those who shall believe
Baptizing in the flowing stream, the sign
Of washing them from guilt of sin to life
Pure, and in mind prepared, if it so chance,
For death, like that which the Redeemer died.
All nations they shall teach; for from that day
Not only to the sons of Abraham’s loins
Salvation shall be preached, but to the sons
Of Abraham’s faith wherever through the world;
So in his seed all nations shall be blessed.
Then to the Heaven of Heavens he shall ascend
With victory, triumphing through the air
Over his foes and yours; there shall surprise
The Serpent, prince of air, and drag in chains
Through all his realm, and there confounded leave;
Then enter into glory, and resume
His seat at God’s right hand, exalted high
Above all names in Heaven; from there he’ll come,
When this world’s dissolution shall be ripe,
With glory and power to judge both quick and dead,
To judge the unfaithful dead, but to reward
His faithful, and receive them into bliss,
Whether in Heaven or earth; for then the earth
Shall all be Paradise, far happier place
Than this of Eden, and far happier days.”
So spoke the archangel Michael, then paused,
As at the world’s great period; and our sire,
Replete with joy and wonder, thus replied:
“O goodness infinite, goodness immense!
That all this good of evil shall produce,
And evil turn to good; more wonderful
Than that which by creation first brought forth
Light out of darkness! Full of doubt I stand,
Whether I should repent now of the sin
By me done and occasioned, or rejoice
Much more, that much more good from it shall spring,
To God more glory, more goodwill to men
From God, and over wrath grace shall abound.
But say, if our deliverer up to Heaven
Must reascend, what will befall the few,
His faithful, left among the unfaithful herd,
The enemies of truth? Who then shall guide
His people, who defend? Will they not deal
Worse with his followers than with him they dealt?”
“Be sure they will,” the angel said; “but from Heaven
He to his own a Comforter will send,
The promise of the Father, who shall dwell,
His Spirit, within them, and the law of faith,
Working through love, upon their hearts shall write,
To guide them in all truth, and also arm
With spiritual armor, able to resist
Satan’s assaults, and quench his fiery darts:
What man can do against them, not afraid,
Though to the death; against such cruelties
With inward consolations recompensed,
And often so upheld as shall amaze
Their proudest persecutors. For the Spirit,
Poured first on his apostles, whom he sends
To evangelize the nations, then on all
Baptized, shall them with wondrous gifts endow
To speak all tongues, and do all miracles,
As did their Lord before them. Thus they win
Great numbers of each nation to receive
With joy the tidings brought from Heaven. At length,
Their ministry performed, and race well run,
Their doctrine and their story written left,
They die; but in their place, as they forewarn,
Wolves shall succeed for teachers, grievous wolves,
Who all the sacred mysteries of Heaven
To their own vile advantages shall turn
Of lucre and ambition, and the truth
With superstitions and traditions taint,
Left only in those written records pure,
Though by the Spirit alone understood.
Then shall they seek to avail themselves of names,
Places and titles, and with these to join
Secular power, though feigning still to act
By spiritual, to themselves appropriating
The Spirit of God, promised alike and given
To all believers; and, from that pretense,
Spiritual laws by carnal power shall force
On every conscience; laws which none shall find
Left them enrolled, or what the Spirit within
Shall on the heart engrave. What will they then
But force the Spirit of Grace itself, and bind
His consort Liberty? What, but unbuild
His living temples, built by faith to stand,
Their own faith, not another’s? For on earth
Who against faith and conscience can be heard
Infallible? Yet many will presume:
From this shall heavy persecution rise
On all who in the worship persevere
Of spirit and truth; the rest, far greater part,
Will deem in outward rites and specious forms
Religion satisfied; Truth shall retire,
Stuck full of slanderous darts, and works of faith
Rarely be found. So shall the world go on,
To good malignant, to bad men benign,
Under her own weight groaning, till the day
Of rest and respite to the just appear,
And vengeance to the wicked, at return
Of him so lately promised to your aid,
The woman’s seed, obscurely then foretold,
Now better known, your Savior and your Lord,
Last in the clouds from Heaven to be revealed
In glory of the Father, to dissolve
Satan with his perverted world, then raise
From the conflagrant mass, purged and refined,
New heavens, new earth, ages of endless date,
Founded in righteousness and peace and love,
To bring forth fruits, joy and eternal bliss.”
He ended; and thus Adam last replied:
“How soon has your prediction, blessed seer,
Measured this transient world, the race of time,
Till time stands fixed! Beyond is all abyss,
Eternity, whose end no eye can reach.
Greatly instructed I shall now depart,
Greatly in peace of thought, and have my fill
Of knowledge, what this vessel can contain;
Beyond which was my folly to aspire.
Henceforth I learn that to obey is best,
And love with fear the only God, to walk
As in his presence, ever to observe
His providence, and on him alone depend,
Merciful over all his works, with good
Still overcoming evil, and by small
Accomplishing great things, by things deemed weak
Subverting worldly strong, and worldly wise
By simply meek; that suffering for truth’s sake
Is fortitude to highest victory,
And to the faithful, death the gate of life;
Taught this by his example whom I now
Acknowledge my Redeemer ever blessed.”
To whom the angel also last replied:
“This having learned, you have attained the sum
Of wisdom; hope no higher, though all the stars
You knew by name, and all the ethereal powers,
All secrets of the deep, all nature’s works,
Or works of God in heaven, air, earth, or sea,
And all the riches of this world enjoyed,
And all the rule, one empire. Only add
Deeds to your knowledge answerable; add faith,
Add virtue, patience, temperance; add love,
By name to come called charity, the soul
Of all the rest: then you will not be loath
To leave this Paradise, but shall possess
A Paradise within you, happier far.
“Let us descend now, therefore, from this top
Of speculation; for the hour precise
Demands our parting now; and see, the guards,
By me encamped on yonder hill, await
Their move; and at their front a flaming sword,
As signal to move out, waves fiercely round.
We may no longer stay. Go, waken Eve;
Her also I with gentle dreams have calmed,
Portending good, and all her spirits composed
To meek submission. At a fitting time
Let her partake with you of what you’ve heard,
Chiefly what may concern her faith to know,
The great deliverance by her seed to come
(For by the woman’s seed) on all mankind,
That you may live, which will be many days,
Both in one faith unanimous, though sad
With cause for evils past, yet much more cheered
With meditation on the happy end.”
He ended, and they both descend the hill.
Descended, Adam to the bower where Eve
Lay sleeping ran ahead, but found her waked;
And thus, with words not sad, she welcomed him:
“From where you come, and where you went, I know;
For God is also in sleep, and dreams advise,
Which he has sent propitious, some great good
Foretelling, since with sorrow and heart’s distress
Wearied I fell asleep. But now lead on;
In me is no delay; with you to go
Is to stay here; without you here to stay
Is to go forth unwilling; you to me
Are all things under Heaven, all places you,
Who for my willful crime are driven out.
This further consolation yet secure
I take from here: though all by me is lost,
Such favor, though unworthy, I am shown,
By me the promised seed shall all restore.”
So spoke our mother Eve, and Adam heard,
Well pleased, but answered not; for now too near
The archangel stood, and from the other hill
To their fixed station, all in bright array,
The cherubim descended, on the ground
Gliding meteorous, as evening mist,
Risen from a river, glides across the marsh
And gathers ground fast at the laborer’s heel
Homeward returning. High in front advanced,
The brandished sword of God before them blazed
Fierce as a comet; which with torrid heat,
And vapor like the burning Libyan air,
Began to parch that temperate clime; at which
In either hand the hastening angel caught
Our lingering parents, and to the eastern gate
Led them direct, and down the cliff as fast
To the subjected plain; then disappeared.
They, looking back, all the eastern side beheld
Of Paradise, so lately their happy seat,
Waved over by that flaming brand, the gate
With dreadful faces thronged and fiery arms.
Some natural tears they dropped, but wiped them soon;
The world was all before them, where to choose
Their place of rest, and Providence their guide:
They hand in hand with wandering steps and slow,
Through Eden took their solitary way.

blocks.p: As one who on a journey stops at noon (1–5). Milton added these five lines in 1674, when he divided the original tenth book into Books XI and XII.
a second stock (7). Noah and his sons, from whom the human race begins again after the Flood.
one shall rise (24). Nimrod, “a mighty hunter before the Lord” and founder of Babel [Gen. 10:8–10]; tradition made him the first king and the builder of the tower.
from rebellion he shall take his name (36). Nimrod’s name was derived from the Hebrew marad, “to rebel.”
liquid pitch (41). Bitumen, which the builders used for mortar [Gen. 11:3]; Milton links its boiling pits with the mouth of Hell.
Confusion (62). Babel, which the Bible connects with the Hebrew word for “confuse” [Gen. 11:9].
right reason (84). The God-given reason that discerns moral truth; for Milton, true liberty cannot exist apart from it.
the irreverent son … Servant of servants (101–104). Ham, who saw his father Noah drunk and naked; Noah cursed Ham’s son Canaan [Gen. 9:20–25].
peculiar (111). Set apart as God’s own possession [Deut. 14:2].
one faithful man (113). Abraham, whose family served other gods beyond the Euphrates [Gen. 12:1–3; Josh. 24:2].
the patriarch … saved from the Flood (117). Noah, who by the biblical chronology lived 350 years after the Flood, into Abraham’s lifetime [Gen. 9:28].
Ur of Chaldea, Haran (130–131). Abraham’s birthplace in Mesopotamia and his first stopping place on the way to Canaan [Gen. 11:31].
Sechem, Moreb (136–137). Shechem and the plain of Moreh, where God first promised Abraham the land [Gen. 12:6–7].

Hamath … Senir (139–146). The bounds of the promised land: Hamath in Syria, Hermon in the northeast, the Mediterranean (“the great western sea”), Mount Carmel on its coast, and Senir, a name for the Hermon range [Num. 34:1–12; Deut. 3:9].
double-fountained stream (144). The Jordan, whose name was thought to join those of its two sources, the Jor and the Dan.
bruise the Serpent’s head (149–150). The first promise of a deliverer, spoken to the serpent in Eden [Gen. 3:15].
A son … a grandchild … a younger son (153–160). Isaac; Jacob, with his twelve sons; and Joseph, who rose to be second only to Pharaoh [Gen. 41:39–44; 46:1–7].
murrain (179). A plague on livestock; the ten plagues of Egypt run through line 190 [Exod. 7–12].
river-dragon (191). Pharaoh, whom Ezekiel calls “the great dragon that lies in the midst of his rivers” [Ezek. 29:3].
cloud and pillar of fire (202–203). The sign of God’s presence that led Israel and stood between them and the Egyptians [Exod. 13:21–22; 14:19–28].
not the readiest way (216). God led Israel the long way round, lest war frighten them back to Egypt [Exod. 13:17].
types and shadows (232–233). Persons, events and rites under the Law that prefigure Christ [Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1].
a mediator (240). The people asked Moses to stand between them and God, and Moses foretold a greater prophet to come [Exod. 20:19; Deut. 18:15; 1 Tim. 2:5].
tabernacle … mercy seat (247–256). The portable sanctuary; the ark held the tablets of the Law beneath a gold lid flanked by cherubim, with the seven-branched lampstand before it [Exod. 25–26].
Sun, in Gibeon stand (265–266). Joshua’s command at the battle of Gibeon; Aialon is Aijalon [Josh. 10:12–13]. “The third from Abraham” is Jacob, renamed Israel [Gen. 32:28].
to prove their natural depravity (287–288). The law exposes and even provokes sin but cannot remove it [Rom. 3:20; 5:20; 7:7–13].
Just for unjust … by faith imputed (294–295). Christ’s righteousness is credited to the believer through faith [1 Pet. 3:18; Rom. 4:22–24; Heb. 10:4].
Joshua, whom the Gentiles Jesus call (310). “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, “the Lord saves” [Heb. 4:8].
The second (321). David, second king of Israel, promised an everlasting throne [2 Sam. 7:12–16; Luke 1:32–33].
seventy years (345). The Babylonian exile [Jer. 25:11]; the “kings, their lords” who allowed the return were the Persian rulers [Ezra 1:1–4].
the priests … a stranger (353–358). In the last centuries before Christ, a priestly family, the Hasmoneans, seized the crown, which then passed to Herod, an Idumaean ruling under Rome.
sages … shepherds (362–367). The wise men and the shepherds at the birth of Jesus [Matt. 2:1–11; Luke 2:8–14].
The Power of the Most High (369). Gabriel’s words to Mary [Luke 1:35]; Adam’s “Virgin mother, hail” (379) echoes the angel’s greeting [Luke 1:28].
capital (383). A pun: deadly, and on the head (Latin caput).
satisfaction (419). The theological term for Christ’s payment of the full penalty that divine justice required for sin [Col. 2:14].
prince of air (454). Satan [Eph. 2:2]; Christ leads the hostile powers captive [Ps. 68:18; Col. 2:15].
quick and dead (460). The living and the dead, as in the Apostles’ Creed [2 Tim. 4:1].
O goodness infinite (469–478). Adam’s wonder that his sin should yield a greater good, the “fortunate fall” of Christian tradition [Rom. 5:20].
Comforter (486). The Holy Spirit [John 14:16–26]; the armor and fiery darts are from [Eph. 6:11–17], the wolves (508) from [Acts 20:29].
meteorous (629). Floating in the air like a meteor, which then meant any airborne phenomenon.
